title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Neonatal seizures constitute a commonly encountered neurologic condition in neonates. [1] Defined as sudden, paroxysmal, and abnormal alterations of electrographic activity from birth to the end of the neonatal period, these events reflect the developmental immaturity of the neonatal brain. This immaturity contributes to a unique pathophysiology and electrographic pattern, resulting in clinical manifestations that can be different and more difficult to identify than in older age groups. [2]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Etiology
content: When seizure activity occurs in a neonate, identifying an underlying and potentially reversible cause is the first and most critical step in evaluation. [6] [7] Etiologies requiring prompt recognition and urgent intervention fall into the following categories: Metabolic disturbances Hypoglycemia [8] Hypocalcemia [9] Hypomagnesemia [10] Hyponatremia Hypernatremia [11] Hypoxic conditions Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy Perinatal asphyxia [12] Intracranial hemorrhage Intraventricular Intraparenchymal Subarachnoid Subdural Infections Bacterial meningitis caused by group B Streptococcus , Escherichia coli , and Listeria monocytogenes [13] [14] Viral encephalitis caused by herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses [15] Intrauterine infection caused by cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, varicella, and Zika virus [16] [17]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Neonatal seizures are a commonly encountered neurologic emergency. [25] [26] In term infants, reported incidence ranges from 1 to 5.5 per 1000 live births, with substantially higher rates observed in preterm populations. [27] [28] [29] The annual incidence in the United States is estimated at 80 to 120 cases per 100,000 neonates.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The neonatal brain differs significantly from that of older age groups. At birth, the brain enters a phase of continued maturation, with many neural structures remaining developmentally immature. This immaturity renders this vital organ vulnerable to pathologic provocation, often manifesting as seizure activity. Seizures involve abnormal, synchronous neuronal discharges within the cerebral cortex. These discharges may result from excessive excitatory input or insufficient inhibitory signaling. An imbalance favoring excitation over inhibition contributes to the increased susceptibility of the neonatal brain to seizures. [30]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Several factors contribute to the excitatory-inhibitory imbalance observed in the neonatal brain. The developmental state of the neonatal neuron is considered the most significant factor. In mature brains, stimulation of the γ-aminobutyric acid receptor produces an inhibitory postsynaptic potential that reduces the likelihood of action potential generation. This effect is achieved by decreasing the cellular membrane potential by modulation of chloride and potassium channels. Chloride influx lowers the membrane potential, counteracting excitatory postsynaptic potentials mediated by glutamate. [31] [32]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: In contrast, the neonatal brain maintains a high intracellular chloride concentration, reversing the chloride ion gradient. Under these conditions, stimulation of the γ-aminobutyric acid receptor leads to chloride efflux and subsequent neuronal depolarization due to sodium and calcium influx. Additional contributors to this imbalance include the earlier development of excitatory synapses relative to inhibitory synapses and the premature maturation of voltage-gated ion channels that promote depolarization.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Obtaining a detailed history and performing a thorough physical examination are essential in neonates presenting with seizures. An underlying provoking cause is frequently present. Therefore, the clinical history should aim to identify relevant risk factors and probable etiologies. These findings help guide both prognosis and treatment strategies. Key historical elements include the timing of seizure onset and maternal, birth, and family history.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Seizures occurring within the first 12 to 24 hours of life are often associated with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, whereas those presenting later may indicate infection, hemorrhage, or stroke. The maternal history should be assessed for acquired and genetic conditions that increase seizure risk. Important considerations include prior miscarriages, suggestive of a genetic syndrome; gestational diabetes, raising the possibility of birth injury or fetal thrombotic vasculopathy; sexually transmitted infections or other vertically transmitted pathogens; prenatal exposure to prescription or illicit drugs; drug withdrawal; and inherited thrombophilias or bleeding disorders. [33] [34]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: The birth history should be evaluated for evidence of anoxic brain injury and intracranial hemorrhage. Clues suggesting anoxic injury include cord prolapse, cord thrombosis, nonreassuring fetal heart rates, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, low Apgar scores, placental abnormalities, and planned home birth. [35] [36] Risk factors for intracranial hemorrhage include birth trauma, operative vaginal delivery, macrosomia, and abnormal fetal presentation, all of which may increase the likelihood of mechanical injury during delivery. [37] The family history should be investigated for early sibling deaths, inborn errors of metabolism, or familial epilepsy syndromes, any of which may suggest an underlying genetic predisposition. [38]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Physical examinations should emphasize findings that may suggest an underlying etiology. Key elements include general appearance, vital signs, head circumference, mental status, level of alertness, and fontanelle contour, particularly when evaluating for bacterial meningitis (with or without septic shock) or acute intracranial hemorrhage. [39] In stable neonates, a complete neurologic examination should focus on cranial nerve function, motor activity, tone, and facial dysmorphisms that may suggest a structural brain lesion, thrombotic event, or genetic disorder. Skin examination should evaluate for stigmata of congenital infection and assess overall perfusion status. [40]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Patients with an inborn error of metabolism may exhibit acute metabolic acidosis, often presenting with lethargy or respiratory distress. Physical findings should be carefully assessed during an ictal event to confirm seizure activity and possibly identify the underlying cause. Focal motor movements may suggest ischemic stroke or localized hemorrhage, whereas generalized motor phenomena raise concern for hypoxic-ischemic injury, infection, or multifocal stroke or hemorrhage.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Focal clonic seizures: Present with repetitive, rhythmic contractions involving the face, limbs, neck, or trunk. These movements cannot be suppressed by repositioning or physical restraint. Seizure activity may migrate during the same ictal event, most commonly to the contralateral hemisphere, though ipsilateral migration can also occur.

content: Generalized clonic seizures: Characterized by diffuse, bilateral, and synchronous motor activity.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Focal tonic seizures: Involve sustained, transient posturing of an extremity, the trunk, or the neck. These seizures may be associated with horizontal eye deviation.

content: Generalized tonic seizures: May mimic decerebrate (extension of both upper and lower extremities) or decorticate (flexion of the upper extremities with extension of the lower extremities) posturing. [41]

content: Myoclonic seizures: Abrupt, nonrepetitive muscle contractions that typically involve the flexor muscle groups of the upper extremities, trunk, diaphragm, or face.

content: Autonomic manifestations, such as sudden changes in vital signs, are uncommon in otherwise healthy neonates. However, these features may indicate subclinical seizure activity in newborns at increased risk for seizures. [43]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: The suspected etiology should direct the diagnostic evaluation of neonatal seizures. Initial assessment should include the prompt exclusion of hypoglycemia—confirmed by bedside blood glucose measurement—and electrolyte disturbances—specifically hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia—using an electrolyte panel. Evaluation for sepsis, meningitis, or encephalitis should include a complete blood count, C-reactive protein, blood cultures, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Neuroimaging using cranial ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging may identify intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, or structural brain abnormalities. Meconium analysis may aid in detecting prenatal exposure to illicit substances. [44]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: EEG is critical to confirm seizure activity, particularly in cases where seizures are subclinical or difficult to detect by bedside observation. [45] [46] Evaluation for inborn errors of metabolism should be considered if seizures are refractory or accompanied by other concerning features. Assessments should include blood gas analysis and targeted metabolic testing, such as serum pyruvate, lactic acid, and urine amino and organic acids. [47] Genetic epilepsy syndromes may also be investigated through molecular testing and epilepsy gene panels as clinically indicated. [48]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: After confirming a patent airway, hemodynamic stability, and intravenous access, treatment should target the underlying cause. Interventions may include therapeutic hypothermia for hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, empiric antibiotics for suspected sepsis or meningitis, intravenous dextrose for severe hypoglycemia, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, or neurosurgical referral for intracranial hemorrhage. [49] In cases of suspected inborn errors of metabolism, initial management comprises discontinuation of enteral feeds, correction of metabolic derangements, and empiric administration of vitamin and cofactor supplements. [50]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Phenobarbital remains the most commonly used first-line antiseizure medication in the setting of clinically apparent, prolonged seizures. [51] Additional boluses may be administered if seizures persist following the initial loading dose. Fosphenytoin is typically used as a second-line agent. [52] Other pharmacologic options include levetiracetam or lidocaine, selected based on the clinical context. Short-acting benzodiazepines, such as midazolam, may be used when definitive treatment is delayed. [53]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: A pediatric neurology consultation should be obtained promptly to guide ongoing management. Neurologists may initiate continuous EEG monitoring to confirm seizure activity, identify subclinical seizures, and assist in managing refractory seizures. [54] [55] These neurologists can also provide recommendations for long-term antiseizure therapy during hospitalization and postdischarge follow-up. The duration of treatment depends on the underlying etiology.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Nonepileptic behaviors should be carefully distinguished from neonatal seizures. [56] These movements can closely resemble epileptic events. Thus, EEG is recommended for accurate characterization. [57] Normal neonatal behaviors that may mimic seizures include sucking motions, hiccuping, and benign neonatal sleep myoclonus, which is physiologic myoclonic activity that occurs during sleep. Other nonepileptic movements, often observed in neonates with systemic illness, include jitteriness, apnea, clonus, tremors, and exaggerated startle responses, such as hyperekplexia. [58] [59]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Motor automatisms, including repetitive eye-opening, eye deviation, oral-buccal movements, bicycling of the limbs, and tonic posturing, may resemble seizure activity but are often triggered by tactile stimulation and suppressed by repositioning or restraint. [60] [61] These manifestations are considered nonepileptic but may reflect underlying neurologic pathology. Further evaluation is warranted if additional concerning features are present. Conditions that may present with seizure-like or seizure-associated phenomena include the following: Anoxia Myoclonus Benign epilepsy syndromes Mitochondrial cytopathies Myoclonic epilepsy Organic acidurias Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy Subdural hematoma Subarachnoid hemorrhage Tuberous sclerosis Viral encephalitis Viral meningitis Vein of Galen malformation Benign neonatal convulsions Cerebellar hemorrhage Herpes simplex encephalitis Myoclonic epilepsy Child abuse Neonatal meningitis Shuddering attacks

content: Accurate differentiation between epileptic and nonepileptic movements is essential to avoid unnecessary treatment and identify neonates requiring further evaluation. EEG confirmation and thorough clinical assessment are crucial for establishing an accurate diagnosis and guiding effective management.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: The underlying etiology largely determines prognosis in neonatal seizures. A normal EEG is associated with excellent outcomes, whereas severely abnormal EEG findings correlate with poor prognosis and an increased risk of cerebral palsy and epilepsy. The presence of interictal spikes on EEG is associated with a 30% risk of developing epilepsy later in life. Reported mortality rates reach up to 20%. Neurological impairment, developmental delay, epilepsy, and long-term disability are frequently observed among survivors of neonatal seizures. [62] [63] [64] [65]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Complications
content: Complications associated with neonatal seizures are frequently associated with the adverse effects of antiseizure medications. Clinicians should monitor for respiratory compromise, particularly hypoxemia and hypercarbia, following administration of benzodiazepines or phenobarbital. [66] Vigilance is essential, as hypoxemia is a common precipitant of cardiac arrest in pediatric patients. [67]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Complications
content: Phenobarbital may cause myocardial depression, whereas phenytoin has been associated with cardiac dysrhythmias. Both these drugs may lead to hemodynamic instability. [68] In such cases, clinicians should be prepared to initiate inotropic support and consider fosphenytoin as a safer alternative to minimize cardiovascular risk. [69] Antiseizure medications may also impair hepatic or renal function, necessitating close monitoring of drug levels during both acute treatment and maintenance therapy. [70]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Complications
content: In addition to medication-related complications, long-term neurologic sequelae may include spastic cerebral palsy, epilepsy, cerebral atrophy with hydrocephalus ex vacuo, and persistent feeding difficulties. Affected neonates often require long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up and coordinated interprofessional care.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Seizures lasting longer than 5 minutes or occurring in rapid succession over several minutes warrant immediate activation of emergency medical services. Emergency antiseizure medications, such as rectal diazepam, may be prescribed for out-of-hospital use. Parents should receive clear instructions on proper administration. [71] Counseling should also address the potential long-term consequences of neonatal seizures, such as the risk of neurologic impairment, and highlight the importance of early referral to rehabilitation services. [72]

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: In children who develop epilepsy, caregivers should remain particularly vigilant in situations where seizures may pose additional risk, such as swimming or activities requiring sustained attention or coordination. [73] Ongoing clinical follow-up with pediatric neurology is essential, and caregivers should be counseled on the critical importance of adherence to prescribed antiseizure therapy. [74]

content: The diagnosis and management of neonatal seizures require an interprofessional approach to prevent complications arising from underrecognition of clinical seizures and adverse effects of antiseizure medications. Early referral to neonatal or pediatric critical care services ensures timely stabilization of oxygenation and hemodynamics and facilitates evaluation by neurocritical care specialists. [75] A pediatric neurology consultation is essential to confirm the diagnosis and guide the treatment strategy.

title: Neonatal Seizure(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: EEG technicians should be readily available to initiate monitoring and detect electrographic seizures that may not present with overt clinical signs. [76] Timely access to antiseizure medications is critical. Pharmacists with expertise in pediatric pharmacology play an important role in ensuring the safe preparation and administration of these agents, particularly in neonatal renal and hepatic immaturity. Bedside nurses are equally vital, as they assist in recognizing clinical seizures, annotating events during monitoring, and safeguarding patients from adverse drug events. [77]
